findings.label: M1
findings.text:
The hint prints the path raw inside a copy-paste shell command, so a hostile or odd file name can inject output and shell syntax (`skills/project-update/update.py:1250-1254`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: I reproduced this in a scratch repo. I tracked `.ai/state/n<LF>l; touch pwn #.jsonl` (it matches `.ai/state/*.jsonl`). The report printed a fake `hint` continuation line, followed by `git rm --cached -- .ai/state/n<LF>l; touch pwn #.jsonl` inside backticks. A path with a space (`a b.jsonl`) also prints a command that untracks the wrong paths (`.ai/state/a` and `b.jsonl`). Anyone who clones a repo can plant such a name, and the output is read by an agent and a human. SKILL.md tells the agent to relay `git rm --cached -- <path>` to the human. The `-z` parsing is correct, but it makes the raw bytes reach stdout and the command line. The change declares "no crash", and it does not crash, but the printed command is wrong or unsafe for any name that needs quoting.
suggested direction: Build the command with `shlex.quote(path)`. Escape control characters in the display (for example `repr`-style or `\n`) so a name cannot start a new `hint` line. Add one test case with a space in the name and one with a newline.

findings.label: L1
findings.text:
The test never exercises a path that needs quoting, and it does not cover a project root that is a subdirectory of a work tree or `--apply` (`tests/test_project_update.py:1428-1461`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: M1 would pass this test. The test covers the main case (positive hint, `--check` exit 0, negative after `git rm --cached`, and no git at all), and the negative case is real: the file stays on disk and is ignored. I ran the subdirectory case by hand and it works, because `ls-files` paths are relative to `-C root`. That case is unpinned. "`--apply` writes nothing for it" is also unpinned, although the code adds no plan item. My manual `--apply` run and a rerun gave exit 0 and "up to date".
suggested direction: Add the subdirectory-root and odd-name assertions to the same test, if cheap. The test's `self.env` copies the whole `os.environ`, so a stray `GIT_DIR` would leak in. This is the same as the existing git tests, so it is not blocking.

findings.label: L2
findings.text:
The wording says "ignored by .gitignore", but `ls-files -ci --exclude-standard` also honours `.git/info/exclude` and the user's global `core.excludesFile` (`skills/project-update/update.py:1238, 1250`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: A file ignored only by a per-machine or global rule is reported as a `.gitignore` problem. That is a cosmetic mismatch in the message. The failure is bounded because the hint is read-only.
suggested direction: Say "ignored by git" or "an ignore rule", or leave as is.

findings.label: L3
findings.text:
The hint prints one long line per file with no cap, and the invalid-UTF-8 decode uses `replace` (`skills/project-update/update.py:1245-1254`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: If a project tracks many ignored files under `.ai/state`, the report floods. Each line repeats about 150 characters of boilerplate. A non-UTF-8 name decodes to U+FFFD, so the printed command points at a path that does not exist. This is an unlikely shape.
suggested direction: Optional. Print the boilerplate once and then the list, or use `os.fsdecode`.

findings.label: L4

But line 47 still says "five version files", and the sync-version docstring says "five places". A reader of the release recipe sees both counts.
suggested direction: Optional wording alignment. The recipe's `git commit -m ... -- <4 files>` is correct, and the path-limited commit also skips unrelated staged changes.

findings.label: L1
findings.text:
edit_json's second RecursionError catch also wraps the migration's own `fn` (`skills/project-update/update.py:697-704`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: a migration bug that raises RecursionError (unbounded recursion in `fn`) is reported as "nested too deeply, so this migration could not run" and holds the schema. Before the change it crashed loudly. The conflict message then blames the user's file for the migration's bug. No shipped migration does this: 0007 is the only `edit_json` caller and its `convert` is not recursive on user data. The code comment names "the migration's edit" as covered, so the trade-off is deliberate.
suggested direction: accept it, or separate `fn` from the copy/compare/dump guard.

findings.label: L2
findings.text:
No test pins the `dump_json(merged)` guard in three_way or the `dump_json(after)` guard in edit_json (`update.py:702`, `update.py:953`)  in_scope: yes
why it matters: the brief asked for a test per path that crashes on the base tree. These two guards are not covered, but the implementer's unreachability claim holds. I measured `dump_json` handling 19000 levels. `deepcopy` fails at 498 levels, `leaf_changes` at 994, and `d == copy.deepcopy(d)` at 497. The only unmeasured step is `merge_json` on differing trees. `json.loads` fails past ~20000 levels, so the `dump_json` guards are defensive only. If `dump_json`'s encoder changes, they are untested.
suggested direction: leave it; the code comment already says guard-only.

findings.label: I1

`read_json` returns None on RecursionError and records a conflict, so 0007 still creates a default `weight.json` (`update.py:632-637`, `migrations/0007_weight_model.py:172-180`)  in_scope: yes
The only caller of `read_json` is 0007 at line 172. With `old=None` and `weight.json` absent, line 180 runs `ctx.create(NEW, template)`. It creates a default table and does not overwrite anything. `risk-tiers.json` is untouched and `MOVES=[]`. The conflict holds the schema through `plan.held` (`update.py:1538`). VERSION is not bumped. The code comment ("None would let a migration create or overwrite what it cannot read") is slightly overstated, because the create still happens. Same behaviour as the existing invalid-JSON case.

`_loads` catches only `(TypeError, ValueError)`. Pre-existing; the base tree crashed earlier at `edit_json`. Goes to the risk register, not to remediation. Severity inside the boundary would be LOW.

why it matters: `_bad` treats null as absent, right on the read side (`x or {}`), wrong on the write side (dict.setdefault returns the existing None). Probed on the working tree: {"axes": null}, {"axes":{"domain":null}}, {"examples": null} → AttributeError NoneType .setdefault; {"axes":{"domain":{"modules":null}}}, {"examples":{"light":null}} → TypeError; {"hints": null} → TypeError not iterable; {"hints":[{"axis":"domain","paths":"x"}]} → AttributeError str.append, "paths": null → TypeError. Same for "tests": null and null reversibility.irreversible/needs_step. Each a Traceback from user JSON once the old table carries a value into that node; nothing written, run aborts. `_new_problem`'s docstring claims coverage it lacks.
suggested direction: on the write side treat a present null as a wrong type; check hints[i].paths is a list or absent; pin one null case and the hints-paths case with a test that crashes on the current tree.
